Open Vision Banana : A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception

Arpit Jadon ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Valentinos Pariza    Jona Ruthardt    Ryousuke Yamada    A. Sophia Koepke    Andrei Bursuc Affiliation: Fundamental AI Lab, University of Technology Nuremberg  DLR  AIST  University of Tübingen, Tübingen AI Center  TUM, MCML  valeo.ai    Yuki M. Asano
Abstract

Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others.

Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M–3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana’s reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model’s image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class–color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color–class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.78.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.015.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code  , as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints .

Project website: openvisionbanana.github.io

  

1 Introduction

Image generation models have become increasingly capable of producing realistic and coherent visual content [44, 102]. A growing line of work argues that this capability reflects general visual understanding that can be utilized for perception tasks [40, 39, 124, 35].

Vision Banana [23] demonstrates that a sufficiently capable image generator can be adapted into a generalist visual perception model by rendering predictions as RGB images. It rivals domain specialists on segmentation and geometry while largely keeping the generator’s editing abilities. However, its base model, data and code are proprietary, so it is unclear which components account for these results. Does the paradigm transfer to publicly available image generators, and how do design choices not elaborated in the Vision Banana report affect the resulting model?

We introduce Open Vision Banana (OVB) , a fully reproducible recipe and set of models for generative visual perception. To derive this recipe, we systematically study the design choices that turn an image generator into a perception model. As shown in Fig. 1, the analysis spans the type and composition of training data, target representations and prompt design, the choice of parameters to adapt, and inference-time readout (decoding generated RGB raw output to task specific final format).

Our experiments show that these choices have large effects and can depend on one another. A model may locate the right region yet score poorly because it paints the wrong color or breaks an output convention. In particular, low-level decisions such as the palette and prompt wording strongly affect accuracy. Supervision for one task can help or hurt others, and choices that help individually may no longer help when combined (Appendix E.2.4).

Finally, we introduce legend ensembling, which segments an image under several randomly drawn color legends and fuses the passes by majority vote. Without retraining, it improves the zero-shot 9B model by up to 8.7 mIoU on Cityscapes and 15.0 mIoU on COCO-Object, with gains mostly from fixing colors bound to wrong classes.

Open Vision Banana makes four main contributions:

  • •

    A fully open recipe for adapting public image generators to four segmentation tasks, depth estimation, and surface normal estimation. The models are trained exclusively on public data, and we release the complete data pipeline, training code, and model checkpoints.

  • •

    Controlled experiments on performance-critical design choices, with an analysis of failure modes.

  • •

    Legend ensembling, a training-free test-time scaling method for generator-based segmentation.

  • •

    Competitive open models that surpass Vision Banana on Cityscapes, come close to it on referring and reasoning segmentation, perform well on depth and surface-normals, and largely retain their editing abilities.

2 Open Vision Banana Recipe

OVB turns a pretrained image generator into a perception model without task-specific heads: given an input image xx and an instruction pp, it generates an RGB image yy that a deterministic, task-specific readout converts into a prediction.

2.1 Base Generators

We release fine-tuned FLUX.2-Klein models at 4B and 9B scale [44], open-weight generators that condition on an input image. All transformer parameters are trained, from the input and context embedders to the output layers. The VAE and text encoder stay frozen.

2.2 RGB Task Modeling

Each task has a deterministic encoder that renders an annotation as an RGB target and a decoder that reads a generated image back into a prediction. Both use per-sample metadata such as the color legend, depth scaling and resizing.

2.2.1 Color Mapping for Segmentation Tasks

Prompts specify colors as RGB triplets, hexadecimal codes (64 most-separated colors of a 200-color palette, Sec. 4.1), or as one of 37 common color names. Black is reserved for background. Prompt templates and color notation vary across samples.

Semantic segmentation.

The prompt lists the requested classes with their colors. Colors are assigned at random for each sample, using the same procedure during training and inference. Given the classes present in an image, training examples request a random subset in 70% of cases, all present classes in 15%, and a subset augmented with absent negative classes in the remaining 15% (Fig. 9). Negative classes teach the model not to hallucinate absent masks. The target paints each prompted class in its assigned color and leaves all other pixels black. At inference, each generated pixel is assigned to the nearest prompted color or to background.

Instance segmentation.

Each prompt names one category and lists 32 colors. We keep the 32 largest instances of the category, sort them by their leftmost pixel and paint the ii-th instance in the ii-th color (Appendix E.1.2). The fixed order makes training targets unique for each image and prompt. Evaluation matches predicted and ground-truth instances by overlap without penalizing alternative color assignments. The readout follows Vision Banana, adding color snapping, gap filling, and GrabCut refinement (Appendix B.2).

Referring segmentation.

Each prompt pairs the referring expression with a color sampled independently from the named palette. The model renders the referred region in that color, which is converted to a binary mask during readout.

2.2.2 Color Mapping for Geometry Tasks

Depth.

Following prior work [6, 38], depth is encoded as affine-invariant inverse depth: valid values are normalized per image to the RGB range and replicated across channels, so nearer points are brighter (figures use a spectral colormap for readability). At inference, the prediction is mapped back to inverse depth and evaluated after per-image affine alignment.

Surface normals.

Normals are converted to a common camera-space convention and each vector component is mapped linearly to one normalized RGB channel. At inference, the RGB prediction is mapped back to camera-space vectors and normalized to unit length.

For both depth and surface-normal tasks, the prompts explicitly state the expected output representation. Further geometric encoding details are provided in Sec. B.1.

2.3 Public Data Mixture

Vision Banana fine-tunes a proprietary base model on proprietary vision data mixed with the base model’s original training data. We only use public datasets. We mix Perception data for the above tasks with replay data from public text-to-image, image-editing, and identity-reconstruction datasets. The resulting pools contain 2.1M training pairs for the zero-shot models and 3.8M for the non-zero-shot models (Appendix C.2). Appendix Tables 20 and 21 give the sampling weight for each task and the datasets and their shares within each task.

2.4 Training

Because all targets are RGB images, we train with the base generator’s rectified-flow objective [55]. The only task-dependent element is the validity mask described below. We encode the target as zyz_{y}, sample Gaussian noise ϵ\epsilon and a uniformly distributed interpolation coefficient t∈(0,1]t\in(0,1], and form

zt=(1−t)​zy+t​ϵ.z_{t}=(1-t)z_{y}+t\epsilon.

Conditioned on the clean image xx and text prompt pp, the transformer predicts v^=vθ​(zt,t,p,x)\hat{v}=v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,p,x) with flow target ϵ−zy\epsilon-z_{y}. Let mjm_{j} indicate whether latent position jj is supervised and CC be the number of latent channels. We use

ℒF​M=𝔼(x,p,y),t,ϵ​[∑jmj​‖v^j−(ϵ−zy)j‖22C​∑jmj].\mathcal{L}_{FM}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,p,y),t,\epsilon}\left[\frac{\sum_{j}m_{j}\left\|\hat{v}_{j}-(\epsilon-z_{y})_{j}\right\|_{2}^{2}}{C\sum_{j}m_{j}}\right]. (1)

Geometry annotations contain undefined regions encoded by placeholder colors that a model might learn to reproduce (Fig. 13). Such regions account for about 8% of target pixels in the non-zero-shot pool and are therefore excluded from the loss using a validity mask. Zero-shot models (2% invalid target regions) and non-geometry tasks use no mask and standard flow-matching. For masked training, the validity mask follows the image transforms and is area-resized to the latent grid; positions with at least 50% valid coverage contribute to the loss. We use no erosion in the final models, exclude samples with no valid latent positions, and normalize each eligible sample by its valid area.

The full-scale models are trained for 100K steps at a global batch size of 192 on aspect-ratio buckets of about 5122512^{2} pixels (×512512\!\times\!512, ×448576\!\times\!448, ×416608\!\times\!416, and their transposes). We use AdamW [57] (weight decay 10−410^{-4}), FSDP, and bf16 autocast with fp32 parameters, using a constant learning rate after linear warmup: ×10−65\!\times\!10^{-6} (500 warmup steps) for 4B and ×10−62\!\times\!10^{-6} (1,000 steps) for 9B. Each epoch draws 1M samples with replacement, split across tasks according to Appendix Table 20. Training thus spans about 19 epochs. Final models use weight-space averaging of a few late transformer checkpoints (Appendix C.1). The non-zero-shot runs took about 73 h on 16 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs (4B) and 79 h on 32 (9B).

2.5 Evaluation Protocol and Data

The evaluation protocol adopts standard metrics for each task and is specified in Appendix C.3. All models sample with 28 steps and a guidance scale of 3.5. The datasets used for evaluation are listed in Appendix Table 21.

3 Evaluating Open Vision Banana

Setup.

We evaluate four OVB models, obtained by fine-tuning FLUX.2 Klein 4B and 9B under two data regimes. Following the dense-prediction literature [128, 40, 38, 110], zero-shot refers to datasets excluded from training, while the tasks themselves are seen during training: the zero-shot models are never trained on any evaluation benchmark. The non-zero-shot models additionally train on the training splits of some of the evaluation datasets (Appendix Table 21) and compute the geometry loss only on valid pixels (Sec. 2.4). Unless noted, segmentation uses the random-draw protocol that re-samples class–color assignments for every image.

Legend ensembling and test-time scaling in brief.

For semantic and instance segmentation, scores marked ⋄ use legend ensembling (details in Sec. 3.4): R passes with different color legends are fused by majority vote, and the mean single-pass score is given in parentheses. Tables report the consensus at a fixed, pre-set number of passes (20 on Cityscapes, 90 on COCO-Object, 11 on SA-Co/Gold), whereas the “up to” gains quoted throughout the paper are the peak of the consensus curve over all evaluated passes (stars in Fig. 5), measured against pass 1.

3.1 Semantic Segmentation Performance

We evaluate on Cityscapes [14] and COCO-Object [49]. All 19 Cityscapes classes fit in one prompt. The 80 categories exceed the 512-token text window that FLUX.2 Klein models are trained with, so each pass splits them into three disjoint groups of 26–27 classes, each prompted in its own sub-pass. Each pass redraws the class partition and the class–color assignments. Legend draws and the generation seed are fixed, so every fine-tuned model sees identical prompts and noise. We compute mIoU at the native evaluation resolution against the GT maps.

Cityscapes. With test-time scaling, the zero-shot (ZS) 9B model reaches 73.9 mIoU (Tab. 1), ahead of the strongest zero-shot specialist (SAM 3, 65.2) and of the generalists Vision Banana (69.9) and non-zero-shot (NZS) SenseNova-Vision (71.2). With target-benchmark data, the non-zero-shot 4B model reaches 76.4 mIoU, the best OVB result. Cityscapes makes up only 0.13% of the non-zero-shot training samples, and the zero-shot models already reach 71.3 (4B) and 73.9 (9B) mIoU without any Cityscapes data. The non-zero-shot recipe improves these results by 5.1 and 1.8 points, respectively, although these differences also reflect other changes to the training mixture and geometry supervision. Most of the accuracy the

COCO-Object. Table 2 compares against recent task specialists that, like OVB, receive the class names and are evaluated on the 80 object classes plus background. With test-time scaling, the zero-shot 9B model surpasses all of them, including the CLIP+SAM pipelines CorrCLIP and OV-Stitcher and the LLaVA-based FSeg-LLaVA, while its mean single pass is on par with the diffusion-based DiffSegmenter and iSeg. Test-time scaling helps far more here than on Cityscapes because, with 80 classes, most errors come from colors bound to the wrong class (Sec. 3.4). Appendix D.1 studies pruning the legend to the classes that an MLLM (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct or Gemma4 31B) judges present in the image.

Qualitative results. Figure 2 show single-pass zero-shot Cityscapes and COCO-Object predictions with the 9B model. Boundaries are sharp and follow object contours, preserving thin structures such as poles or bicycle frames.

3.2 Referring and Reasoning Segmentation

We use the referring interface of Sec. 2.2 and report cIoU on RefCOCOg val (UMD) and gIoU on ReasonSeg val (Appendix C.3). RefCOCOg expressions are passed to OVB unchanged. For ReasonSeg, we use Gemma4 31B to rewrite each query into an explicit referring expression. Tab. 5 also reports results on the raw queries and with rewrites by Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking [3] and Gemini 3.1 Pro.

ReasonSeg.

With query rewriting, the zero-shot 4B model reaches 67.9 gIoU (Tab. 4), outperforming zero-shot SegZero and RSVP-GPT-4o, as well as the target-trained LISA and SenseNova-Vision. SAM 3 and Vision Banana score higher, but both use Gemini 2.5 Pro as their reasoner and SAM 3 also uses it to refine its masks iteratively. Table 5 disentangles the contributions of the base model, fine-tuning, and query rewriting. Even with Gemma4 rewriting, F2K4B Base reaches only 24.1 gIoU, whereas frozen Nano Banana Pro, the base of Vision Banana, already reaches 70.2 on raw queries [18], close to zero-shot OVB. Rewriting adds 26.7 gIoU to the fine-tuned model but only 5.6 to the pretrained one, so explicit expressions pay off only once fine-tuning has taught the model to segment. The non-zero-shot recipe improves the 4B model more on raw queries (41.2 to 51.2) than with Gemma4 rewriting (67.9 to 74.6), suggesting that it partly learns to resolve implicit queries itself. Replacing Gemma4 with Gemini 3.1 Pro leaves the non-zero-shot 4B model unchanged at 74.6 gIoU. The choice of reasoner therefore matters much less than the perception ability of the base generator.

RefCOCOg.

The zero-shot 9B model reaches 57.4 cIoU (Tab. 4), ahead of zero-shot HybridGL but behind LocalizationHeads-LLaVA, SAM 3 with Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Vision Banana. OVB resolves long compositional expressions without a dedicated grounding module, whereas the stronger entries use an MLLM to interpret the expression or, in the case of Vision Banana, build on Nano Banana Pro, a proprietary generator of undisclosed but probably larger size. With the target training splits (non-zero-shot regime), the 9B model reaches 69.2 cIoU.

Qualitative results. Even on raw ReasonSeg queries, OVB often segments the region that the query implies (Fig. 3). On RefCOCOg, OVB follows object outlines more tightly than the ground truth (Fig. 18 in the appendix).

3.3 Instance Segmentation Performance

We use the instance interface of Sec. 2.2 and report cgF1, IL-MCC, and pmF1 on SA-Co/Gold (Appendix C.3). A Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct presence gate decides whether the queried category is present before OVB paints its instances. The readout is described in Sec. B.2. SenseNova-Vision evaluation uses the same gate and a panoptic prompt naming only the query, dropping instances with other labels as in its benchmark parsing. The model is non-zero-shot, since it trains on SA-1B images used by one SA-Co/Gold subset.

Results.

With legend ensembling over 11 passes, the zero-shot 9B model reaches 37.4 cgF1 (Tab. 6, mean single pass 36.0), ahead of OWLv2, DINO-X, and APE-D and almost 3 times the score of Gemini 2.5. The non-zero-shot SAM 3 and Vision Banana remain ahead (54.1 and 47.5). Ensembling raises the non-zero-shot 9B model from 38.1 to 39.6 cgF1, and the Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B gate lifts the two ensembled scores to 37.9 and 40.1. Figure 2 shows zero-shot predictions on SA-Co/Gold, where instances of the same category receive distinct colors even when they overlap or are partially occluded.

3.4 Test-time Scaling through Legend Ensembling

Legend ensembling varies the class–color legend in the prompt across RR passes over the same image while keeping the generation seed fixed. Each pass is read out with its own legend, and the resulting class maps are fused by per-pixel majority vote (see Fig. 4). A black pixel is a vote for the background class on COCO-Object and no vote on Cityscapes, which has no background class. For instance segmentation, each pass permutes the 32 instance colors. Since these colors carry no class identity, voting operates on the refined binary masks of each pass (Appendix B.2). Masks from different passes that overlap with IoU≥0.5\mathrm{IoU}\geq 0.5 are grouped into one instance. An instance is kept if it appears in at least half of the passes, and its final mask contains the pixels covered by at least half of them. No ground-truth is used.

Scaling behavior.

Under legend ensembling, majority-vote consensus improves as passes increase (Fig. 5, dashed lines show single passes). On Cityscapes, the 9B model climbs quickly from 65.4 mIoU (pass 1) and saturates at about 74 mIoU after 10–15 passes, whereas COCO-Object, with 80 classes, keeps improving over many more passes. On SA-Co/Gold, each prompt names one category, so there are fewer binding errors to correct and the gain is smaller but ensembling still improves the 9B model from 36.0 to 37.5 cgF1. Figure 7 shows how the predictions evolve as the number of passes grows.

Color binding and region segmentation errors.

As a diagnostic, we relabel each predicted connected region with its majority ground-truth class (oracle in Tab. 7). The oracle score is high from early in training while the standard score keeps rising, so OVB learns to delineate regions well before it reliably paints them in the prompted colors. For the final 9B model, the oracle score far exceeds the single-pass score on Cityscapes (85.9 vs. 65.4 mIoU). Ensembling raises the standard score to 73.9 while the oracle score stays at 85.6, suggesting that much of the gain comes from correcting class–color bindings and the regions themselves barely change. Single-pass errors are commonly of three kinds: whole regions bound to a wrong class, unassigned pixels left black, and small speckles along object contours, where blended colors are read out as a wrong class. Legend ensembling reduces all three (see Fig. 7).

Class-wise gains and uncertainty.

Figure 6 shows that the benefit is largest for infrequent and thin classes, which have the least stable color assignments in a single pass (e.g., “train” gains +34.4+34.4 IoU), while large, frequent classes improve little. Moreover, the agreement across passes provides empirical per-pixel confidence estimates. The 6% of Cityscapes pixels with agreement below 0.9 account for 58% of all errors and are concentrated near object boundaries (Appendix D.2, Fig. 10).

3.5 Performance on Geometry Tasks

Table 8 compares the same four selected models on full depth and normal benchmarks. We evaluate depth on the five benchmark splits in Appendix D.3, fitting a scale and shift to the ground-truth disparity for each image. Marigold V2 aligns in log-depth. Normals use the fixed camera-facing RGB convention, without test-image axis fitting. Published specialist scores retain their original training data and preprocessing and are reference values; Vision Banana’s metric-depth scores are not directly comparable with our aligned relative-depth scores.

Depth.

The non-zero-shot models improve depth on NYUv2 and ScanNet for both model sizes, and on ScanNet come close to the published specialist scores. Both zero-shot models remain stronger on KITTI. DIODE shows a mixed result: non-zero-shot training lowers 4B AbsRel but reduces its threshold accuracy, while the 9B model loses on both metrics (Appendix Table 24). The 9B zero-shot example in Fig. 8 recovers the room layout, although fine boundaries remain softer than the ground truth.

Surface normals.

The non-zero-shot models lower mean angular error on NYUv2 and Sintel, but increase it on ScanNet and iBims-1 (Tab. 8). For 9B, mean error falls from 19.85∘19.85^{\circ} to 13.51∘13.51^{\circ} on NYUv2 and from 20.53∘20.53^{\circ} to 11.43∘11.43^{\circ} on DIODE indoor (Appendix Table 25).

3.6 Retention of Generation Abilities

In terms of image generation, no training mixture contains data from the generation benchmarks, so all four models are zero-shot on them.

Image editing.

The examples in Appendix Fig. 14 show instruction-following edits that preserve unrelated image regions. OVB prefixes editing prompts with [TASK: IMAGE_EDITING]. Adding the same prefix to the base models barely changes their ImgEdit-Bench [114] scores (Tab. 9), supporting the attribution of score differences to fine-tuning. Perception fine-tuning improves the 4B Basic average over its base model (3.66 →\to 3.78 and 3.82 for the zero-shot and non-zero-shot mixes), mainly through the remove edit type (Appendix Table 26), and retains the 9B Basic average (3.89 vs. 3.86 and 3.89). Retention is less consistent on the 50-prompt UGE suite: the 9B non-zero-shot model drops from the base model’s 4.03 to 3.68, despite matching its Basic score.

Text-to-image generation.

On GenAI-Bench (Tab. 10), we score all 1600 prompts with VQAScore [47], using CLIP–FlanT5 as the judge over three generation seeds, with base and fine-tuned models sharing the same per-prompt noise. Our perception fine-tuning lowers VQAScore for all four models. The drop is smaller for 9B than for 4B (−0.030 vs. −0.050 with the zero-shot mixture) and slightly smaller with the non-zero-shot mixture (−0.027 and −0.049). The selected examples in Fig. 14 in the Appendix show successful text rendering and object counts.

3.7 Feature Quality

We also test whether generative perception tuning improves the backbone’s frozen features for downstream vision tasks. We probe the features of single-stream block 6 (4B) and 3 (9B), extracted with an empty prompt at noise level 0.7, and, as in DINOv3 [85], keep the better of the pre- and post-normalization features. We evaluate unsupervised object discovery with TokenCut [97] on COCO20k [90], following the standard Correct Localization (CorLoc) protocol, and geometric and semantic correspondence on ScanNet and SPair-71k [63] with Probe3D [19] (Tab. 11). Fine-tuning improves all three for both model sizes: object discovery by +8.3+8.3 (4B) and +3.8+3.8 (9B) CorLoc, geometric correspondence by up to +13.1+13.1 R@5, and semantic correspondence by up to +2.6+2.6 R@0.1. OVB 9B even surpasses DINOv3 7B in object discovery (56.3 vs. 54.8) and semantic correspondence (61.9 vs. 56.1). Learning to output dense perception maps thus sharpens how well the backbone’s features localize objects and match points across images. Appendix Fig. 15 shows that the fine-tuned features localize objects that the pretrained features miss or only partly cover, and their similarity maps are less noisy and better follow the object outline.

4 Analysis of Design Choices

In this section, we analyze critical design choices during task definition, data acquisition, and model training to derive the final recipe for generative visual perception (Fig. 1). Each analysis varies one factor and keeps other settings as described below.

Training.

The analyses use two reduced setups, one for segmentation and one for geometry. Each variant fine-tunes F2K9B Base with the full-scale 9B setup (Sec. 2.4) for 37.5K steps, at a global batch size of 64 (segmentation) or 8 (geometry). A segmentation run takes about 370 GPU-hours on GH200 GPUs (23 h on 16 GPUs), and a geometry run about 80 GPU-hours on H200 GPUs (20 h on 4 GPUs).

Data.

Training examples follow the segmentation and geometry mixtures in Appendix Table 20. Each epoch draws about 250K (segmentation) or 160K (geometry) samples, so the 2.4M and 300K samples seen during training amount to 9.6 and 1.9 epochs. Segmentation sampling is without replacement; geometry sampling follows source quotas and uses replacement when a source is too small (Appendix C.2).

Evaluation.

Segmentation variants are evaluated on the segmentation benchmarks in Appendix Table 21. For the geometry ablations, we additionally report five evaluations of other tasks to check whether a gain in depth or normals comes at the cost of the model’s other capabilities: Cityscapes mIoU (CS), COCO-Stuff mIoU (CO), RefCOCOg cIoU (RS), SA-Co/Gold-14K cgF1 (IS), and the ImgEdit UGE score (IE). Cityscapes and RefCOCOg use the full validation splits, and COCO-Stuff and SA-Co/Gold use fixed subsets (C.4). Appendix C.3 gives the full evaluation protocol.

4.1 Task Definition

We first study how to express the tasks as RGB images. Additional analysis can be found in Appendix E.

RQ-S1. Which class–color mappings let the model generalize and follow the prompt?

Setup.

To test whether a model memorizes a fixed class–color mapping (e.g., ‘car’→\rightarrowblue) or learns to follow the colors given in the prompt, we vary the mapping at training and evaluation time, using the 19 Cityscapes classes shared by all datasets in this experiment. Fixed colors (#1) always lists all 19 classes with fixed color–class correspondences, random colors (#2) lists all 19 classes with new colors for every sample, and random subset (#3) lists only a random subset of present classes, leaving unlisted regions black (Fig. 9). Random colors are drawn from the 100 most-separated colors of our palette with a minimum pairwise color difference of Δ​E=25\Delta E=25 (Euclidean distance in CIELAB, CIE76), relaxed when too few colors satisfy it, or from the 37-color named palette when a prompt uses color names (Sec. 4.1). Distance requirement is relaxed when fewer than required colors satisfy the filtering criteria. Each variant fine-tunes F2K9B Base for 6K steps at batch size 64 on a 40K-sample pool of 25% semantic segmentation (BDD100K and ACDC), 25% identity reconstruction and 50% image editing.

Analysis.

As shown in Tab. 12, training with fixed colors performs well under the same evaluation protocol (53.9 mIoU), but collapses when the colors are varied at inference (7.1), indicating rigid memorization of the mapping. Training with random colors (#2) avoids this collapse and reaches 51.0 mIoU with unseen color assignments. In the set protocol, the prompt lists only a subset of the classes and unrequested regions are not scored (Appendix C.3), so it tests whether the model follows the legend. Random subset performs best here (66.5 mIoU) but loses 15.0 mIoU under the random-draw (rd) protocol, where all Cityscapes classes are requested.

RQ-S2. What color palette best supports unambiguous color generation for semantic segmentation?

Setup.

We construct a 200-color palette from Matplotlib’s XKCD colors using farthest-point sampling in CIELAB space and order colors from most to least separated. We compare the full palette with its first 100, 64 and 32 colors and a per-image variant that uses the NN most-separated colors, where NN is the number of classes present in the image, or the number of listed classes if the prompt adds absent ones. For each training and evaluation sample, colors are drawn from the corresponding palette and randomly assigned to the requested classes. Smaller palettes offer fewer colors but larger distances between them.

Analysis.

Restricting the palette to more widely separated colors generally improves segmentation over using all 200 colors, particularly on COCO-Stuff and COCO-Things. Shrinking the palette further does not always help: Top 32 improves Cityscapes but lowers both COCO benchmarks. Top 64 achieves the highest mean over the six settings (54.5 mIoU) and becomes the default. Appendix E.1.1 evaluates this model with a varying requested classes per image and finds that mIoU drops as more classes are requested.

4.2 Training Data

RQ-D1. How do image-generation and image-editing data affect geometry and retained capabilities?

Setup.

We vary the share of image-generation examples and, separately, editing and identity-reconstruction examples. Each share is set to zero, half its default, its default, or twice its default, with the remaining sampling probability redistributed across the other tasks. The defaults are 15% and 25%, respectively. All variants train for 50K steps.

Analysis.

No setting is best for all tasks, and trends are not monotonic (Tab. 14). Removing generation data gives the lowest normal error but worsens depth. Doubling it to 30% raises depth AbsRel from 0.061 to 0.063, slightly increases δ1\delta_{1} from 96.5% to 96.6%, and worsens both normal errors. Removing editing/identity data worsens both geometry tasks and sharply reduces editing retention. The variant without generation examples also gives the highest GenAI-Bench CLIP–FlanT5 score in this sweep (0.8074 versus 0.7871 at the 15% default; Appendix Table 31(d)). Editing and identity-reconstruction examples remain in its training mixture. Increasing the generation share to 30% provides no consistent improvement over the 15% default. The 15% generation / 25% editing/identity control ranks first or second on seven of nine metrics in each panel.

4.3 Architecture

RQ-A1. Which model components should be tuned?

Setup.

We progressively increase the fraction of the F2K9B Base transformer updated during fine-tuning, from only the last few single-stream blocks to all transformer parameters. Full except embeddings updates all transformer parameters except the input and context embeddings, while full transformer additionally adapts those embeddings.

Analysis.

Tuning only the last few blocks falls behind on every task except editing (Tab. 15). Freezing only the embeddings gives the lowest depth error and the best instance score, whereas full-transformer adaptation gives the lowest normal error. The final models update the full transformer, which is best or second best on every task except editing.

Appendix E.3 studies low-rank adaptation of the 4B model as a low-compute alternative: adapters of rank 64–128 match full fine-tuning on editing, depth and normals, but trail it by about 12 mIoU on semantic segmentation.

5 Related Work

Pretrained image generators are increasingly used for visual perception, either by extracting their semantic and geometric features [125, 108] or by framing vision tasks directly as image prediction [4, 95, 96, 27]. Specialized models such as Marigold and Lotus further exploit generative priors for dense geometric prediction [38, 32], but do not aim at preserving the general-purpose generation abilities.

More closely related are generalist models that unify generation and perception. DICEPTION [124], Jodi [109], OneDiffusion [46], and PixWizard [50] adapt diffusion-based generators to multiple vision tasks, while SenseNova-Vision [31] and MODUS [113] build on unified multimodal architectures. Vision Banana [23] demonstrates strong multi-task perception through instruction-tuning a proprietary image generator while retaining its generative capabilities. Other studies find that frozen generators can already solve some perception tasks out-of-the-box [111, 54]. OVB differs from these works in that every component is public and in its controlled analysis of critical design choices. An extended discussion is provided in Appendix A.

6 Conclusion

Open Vision Banana is a fully open recipe for turning pretrained image generators into unified segmentation and geometry models while largely preserving their editing abilities. Controlled experiments favor randomized, well-separated color palettes, relative inverse depth, full transformer adaptation, and highlight a trade-off between perception accuracy and retained generation quality. The resulting models are competitive across tasks, improve further with training-free legend ensembling, and yield stronger frozen features for object discovery and correspondence. Their main limitation is the weaker perception of open base models relative to proprietary generators such as Nano Banana Pro. We release data pipelines, code, and weights to promote further research.

Appendix A Extended Related Work

Generative image models as visual priors.

Image generators have evolved from text-to-image synthesis systems into flexible image-to-image engines through latent diffusion, transformer-based diffusion backbones, instruction tuning, and controllable conditioning [77, 71, 8, 123, 104]. This has motivated a growing line of work that reuses generative priors to solve perception tasks instead of training separate discriminative models. Early diffusion-perception methods such as VPD [125], ODISE [108], and TADP [42] showed that pretrained diffusion features and denoising pipelines contain spatially aligned semantic and geometric information useful for segmentation, depth, and dense prediction. These methods typically train perception heads on the extracted features or modify the architecture, so the prediction is not produced by the generator itself.

Vision tasks as image generation.

A second line of work frames vision tasks directly as image generation. Early methods show that masks, depth maps, and other perception outputs can be represented as RGB images [96, 98, 27, 24]. More recent contributions exploit strong visual priors acquired by generative foundation models during large-scale pretraining for dense prediction, mostly depth and surface normals [38, 39, 28, 22, 112, 106, 32, 33, 94]. Several concurrent works study segmentation-specific uses of generative models [92, 1, 40, 117]. These models usually address one or a few tasks and do not try to preserve or evaluate general image generation.

Unified generation and understanding.

The idea of unifying heterogeneous vision tasks through a shared image-space prediction interface predates the recent wave of generative foundation models. Early works such as Visual Prompting via Image Inpainting [4] and Painter [95] formulated diverse computer-vision tasks as image prediction. More recently, this idea has been revisited in the context of pretrained generative models that unify generation and understanding. DICEPTION [124] is one of the closest open baselines, using color-encoded perception targets in a diffusion model. Vision Banana [23] demonstrates that instruction-tuning Nano Banana Pro on vision-task data can turn a generator into a strong generalist perception model without sacrificing its original generation abilities. Generally, unified multimodal systems differ mainly in the generative backbone they adapt. Jodi [109], OneDiffusion [46], PixWizard [50], and UniPercept [126] build on diffusion- or flow-based image generators and model perception outputs as images, labels, or task-specific visual representations. SenseNova-Vision [31] and MODUS [113] instead adapt BAGEL-style [16] unified multimodal decoders, combining autoregressive text generation with a shared flow-matching visual generation pathway for producing dense RGB outputs through VAE latents. Relatedly, RINO [111] and other recent works [54, 18] show that off-the-shelf image generation or editing models already possess substantial dense-prediction capabilities without perception-specific adaptation or retraining, though they typically underperform tuned approaches and rely on adjusted evaluation protocols to become competitive. OVB adapts pretrained flow-matching generators using only public data, releases its training code and weights, and ablates the design choices that proprietary systems leave unspecified. An overview of related works is provided in Tab. 16.

Appendix B RGB Task Encoding and Readout Details

B.1 Semantic-Seg, Depth, and Normal Encoding

Semantic segmentation.

Figure 9 shows one training image under the three class–color mappings compared in Sec. 4.1. The released recipe uses randomized colors and mixes subset, full-set (all classes present in the image), and negative-class prompts (Sec. 2.2.1).

Depth.

We first convert each source to camera-zz depth ziz_{i} in meters. The default target is inverse depth di=1/zid_{i}=1/z_{i}, normalized using the minimum and maximum valid inverse depths in each image: pi=(di−dmin)/(dmax−dmin)p_{i}=(d_{i}-d_{\min})/(d_{\max}-d_{\min}). We replicate pip_{i} over RGB, so nearer points are brighter. Constant-depth images receive pi=0.5p_{i}=0.5. This encoding discards metric scale and evaluation uses disparity-affine alignment (Sec. C.3).

The metric-RGB ablation instead maps camera-zz depth in meters to t⁡(z)=1−(1+z/10)−2t(z)=1-(1+z/10)^{-2} and then to the fixed RGB-cube path of Vision Banana [23]. The decoder projects each generated color onto the nearest path segment and inverts tt.

Surface normals.

We convert every source to unit camera-space vectors with +x+x image-right, +y+y image-up, and +z+z toward the camera. The canonical RGB encoding is

(R,G,B)=((1−x)/2,(1+y)/2,(1+z)/2).(R,G,B)=((1-x)/2,(1+y)/2,(1+z)/2). (2)

Before training, we resolve each dataset’s stored axes and signs, interpolate the vector components and re-normalize before RGB encoding. Because the encoding is affine, bilinearly interpolating RGB before decoding and normalization gives the same vectors as interpolating and re-normalizing the vector components, apart from RGB quantization. The evaluation procedure is given in Sec. C.3. Horizontal augmentation flips the image and negates the physical xx component before re-encoding, preserving the image-right convention.

B.2 Instance-segmentation inference and readout

Training targets.

When the queried category is present in a training example, we keep the 32 largest instance masks of that category (the cap applies only to training targets), rank them left-to-right by their first foreground pixel with ties broken top-to-bottom, and paint the ii-th mask in the ii-th prompt color on a black background. Prompt and target therefore always agree on which instance gets which color. Negative examples without the queried category use the same 32-color prompt with an all-black target.

RGB-to-instance decoder.

If the presence gate judges the queried category absent, no prediction is emitted. Otherwise, we first snap the generated image to the palette: at the generation resolution, every pixel takes the nearest of the 33 allowed colors (black and the 32 palette colors) in Euclidean RGB distance. Legend ensembling only permutes the order of the 32 colors across passes, so every pass snaps to the same 33 colors. The snapped image is then resized to the ground-truth resolution with nearest-neighbor interpolation, which introduces no blended colors, and decoded. Let y^​(u)∈[0,255]3\hat{y}(u)\in[0,255]^{3} be the snapped RGB value at pixel uu, and let cbg=(0,0,0)c_{\mathrm{bg}}=(0,0,0). We first define the foreground as

ℱ={u:‖y^​(u)−cbg‖22≥τ2}.\mathcal{F}=\left\{u:\left\|\hat{y}(u)-c_{\mathrm{bg}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\geq\tau^{2}\right\}. (3)

We use τ=58\tau=58; the same τ\tau also sets the color-bin width and the merge threshold below. Pixels outside ℱ\mathcal{F} are treated as background. Each foreground RGB channel is quantized as qj​(u)=⌊y^j​(u)/τ⌋q_{j}(u)=\lfloor\hat{y}_{j}(u)/\tau\rfloor, and 8-connected components are extracted separately within each resulting three-dimensional color bin. After snapping, τ\tau thus mainly decides which nearby palette colors are grouped, so fragments of one instance painted in neighboring palette colors can still be joined.

Each candidate component SS then passes two filtering stages. First, we discard it when |S|<θsize​H​W\lvert S\rvert<\theta_{\mathrm{size}}HW, where θsize=8×10−4\theta_{\mathrm{size}}=8\times 10^{-4} and H,WH,W are the image height and width. Second, using a 3×33\times 3 binary erosion E⁡(S)E(S), we discard thin boundary artifacts when |E⁡(S)|/|S|<θerosion=0.1\lvert E(S)\rvert/\lvert S\rvert<\theta_{\mathrm{erosion}}=0.1. We subsequently connect two surviving components when their mean RGB values are sufficiently similar and their joint bounding box is sufficiently compact:

‖c¯a−c¯b‖22\displaystyle\left\|\bar{c}_{a}-\bar{c}_{b}\right\|_{2}^{2} ≤τ2,\displaystyle\leq\tau^{2}, (4)
A⁡(B⁡(Sa∪Sb))\displaystyle A\!\left(B(S_{a}\cup S_{b})\right) ≤γ⁡[A⁡(B⁡(Sa))+A⁡(B⁡(Sb))].\displaystyle\leq\gamma\!\left[A(B(S_{a}))+A(B(S_{b}))\right].

Here, B⁡(⋅)B(\cdot) denotes an axis-aligned bounding box, A⁡(⋅)A(\cdot) its area, and γ=1\gamma=1. The final instance masks are the connected components of this merge graph, and component colors and bounding boxes are not updated while merging. This procedure repairs nearby fragments of a painted instance, while the bounding-box constraint discourages direct merging of spatially distant same-colored fragments.

Gap filling and boundary refinement.

Let y~\tilde{y} be the raw generated image, nearest-neighbor resized to the ground-truth resolution. A pixel uu outside every decoded mask with ∥y~​(u)−cbg∥2≥τ\lVert\tilde{y}(u)-c_{\mathrm{bg}}\rVert_{2}\geq\tau joins the nearest decoded instance if it lies within 3 pixels of it. Each mask MM is then refined with GrabCut [78], run on the input image bilinearly resized to the ground-truth resolution and cropped to the bounding box of MM enlarged by 15 pixels on each side. Let M−M^{-} and M+M^{+} be MM eroded and dilated by 3 pixels with a 3×33\times 3 kernel. GrabCut is initialized with M−M^{-} as sure foreground, M∖M−M\setminus M^{-} as probable foreground, M+∖MM^{+}\setminus M as probable background, and the rest of the crop as sure background. After two iterations, the result replaces MM only if it keeps at least 90% of |M|\lvert M\rvert; MM is also kept when its eroded core is empty. OpenCV runs single-threaded with its random seed fixed per query and pass. Every pass is refined independently before the vote of Sec. 3.4. The instance-prompt ablation of Sec. E.1.2 uses the same decoder.

The resulting instance masks are scored with the SA-Co/Gold protocol described in Sec. C.3.

Appendix C Implementation Details

This section details the training configurations, training data, and evaluation of all models. Unless stated otherwise, each ablation changes only the variable it studies.

C.1 Training configurations

Table 17 gives the training configuration of the full-scale models, and Table 18 those of the segmentation and geometry ablations.

Model averaging.

Each final model averages the transformer weights of two to five checkpoints from the last 20K steps of training, selected by their overall performance on the evaluation benchmarks. The exact steps and weights are listed with the released models. Table 19 compares the averaged zero-shot 9B model with its final 100K checkpoint under matched settings: gains are modest, within one point on every task.

C.2 Training data

Table 21 lists the full-scale training pool and the evaluation datasets, and Table 20 gives the per-task sampling weights of the full-scale (OVB) and ablation mixtures.

Full-scale training data.

The zero-shot OVB models use the non-underlined sources in Table 21, excluding target-benchmark training splits and evaluation images. The five geometry sources (Synscapes, Replica, Matterport3D, Hypersim and Taskonomy) cover rendered street scenes and synthetic, reconstructed and scanned interiors. We convert all sources to the conventions of Sec. B.1.

Non-zero-shot models also use the underlined sources and their training splits, which grows the pool from 2.1M to 3.8M training pairs. For VKITTI2, training uses non-clone renderings of the five scenes used for normal evaluation. Training and test images therefore show the same scenes under different rendering conditions.

For geometry sources added to the non-zero-shot pool, we identify contiguous border rows and columns with at least half their pixels invalid. We crop these from the image, target and mask, unless the crop would remove more than 25% at any edge or retain less than 60% of the image area. After this step, we discard examples with more than 25% invalid area. Remaining invalid regions inside the image are excluded from the loss by the validity mask.

The non-zero-shot Replica pool contains 3,341 upright views rendered with mesh vertex colors; the zero-shot models use the earlier pool. For the added ScanNet source, we fit local planes to depth to obtain normals and orient them toward the camera. Released manifests record source versions, counts, image IDs and crop coordinates.

Ablation training data.

The ablations draw from smaller subsets of the zero-shot pool and follow the same exclusions.

  • •

    Segmentation ablations use no geometry data. They use the non-underlined 2D sources but leave out Hypersim (semantic and instance segmentation) as well as RailSem19 and Trans10K-v2 (semantic segmentation). Referring segmentation uses 150K samples from Visual Genome (without COCO images) and Mapillary Vistas.

  • •

    Geometry ablations restrict the 2D tasks to ACDC, BDD100K, ADE20K, and PASCAL VOC for semantic segmentation and to ADE20K, Mapillary Vistas, and PASCAL VOC for instance segmentation. The depth and normal weights are each split equally among the five non-underlined geometry sources. The depth- and normal-prompt variants of the prompt study assign the full 30% geometry share to a single geometry task. Editing replay uses the first 50K valid Pico-Banana pairs after shuffling, identity replay uses 10K of their source images as both input and target, and text-to-image replay uses 500K PD12M examples. All three selections use seed 42. Each geometry-ablation epoch draws 160K examples across all tasks according to the task weights.

C.3 Evaluation details and metrics

Our evaluation protocol follows Vision Banana [23] where applicable and extends it to a broader benchmark suite. The exact datasets used for evaluation are listed in Table 21.

Generation.

We compare each final model with its base generator using matched inference and judging settings, with 28 steps and guidance 3.5. GenAI-Bench [47] uses VQAScore with the CLIP–FlanT5 [XXL] judge, for the final models and the geometry ablations alike (IG-C, Table 31); ImgEdit-Bench [114] uses ImgEdit-Judge. Both results are averaged over three generation seeds. Editing uses a fixed assignment to 16 logical shards because the noise generator advances between examples within each shard.

Semantic segmentation.

Mean intersection-over-union (mIoU), computed as the arithmetic mean of the per-class IoUs is used for evaluation. We consider three evaluation protocols. Fixed uses the complete dataset taxonomy with its canonical class–color mapping. Random-draw (rd) retains the complete taxonomy but samples a new class–color mapping for each image, thereby measuring generalization across colors. Set requests a random subset of the classes present in each image and assigns them random colors. Its size is drawn uniformly between 1 and one fewer than the number of present classes, or is 1 if only one class is present. Only the requested classes are scored and pixels of other classes are ignored, so this protocol measures how accurately the model paints the requested classes, without penalizing painting in unrequested regions. Unless otherwise stated, we use random-draw evaluation throughout the paper.

Referring segmentation.

Following LISA [45], we report cumulative IoU (cIoU), the summed foreground intersection divided by the summed foreground union over all queries, and gIoU, the mean per-query foreground IoU. cIoU weights queries by their union area, whereas gIoU gives every query equal weight.

Instance segmentation.

We use the official SA-Co/Gold evaluator of SAM 3, as Vision Banana does. It retains only queries that are instance-exhaustive in all three oracle annotations. Each decoded instance (Sec. B.2) is exported as a binary COCO RLE mask with confidence 1.0, so the evaluator’s 0.5 score threshold discards nothing. Queries that the VLM presence gate judges absent receive no prediction, Vision Banana filters queries the same way with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite. For each query, we score the same predictions against all three annotations and keep the result with the highest local F1, averaged over the IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05. An empty prediction for an empty target counts as perfect. Evaluation uses all ground-truth instances, without the training cap of 32. Positive micro-F1 (pmF1) measures instance matching and mask localization on positive queries. Image-level Matthews correlation coefficient (IL-MCC) measures category-presence accuracy. Within each subset, cgF1=pmF1×IL​-​MCC\mathrm{cgF1}=\mathrm{pmF1}\times\mathrm{IL\text{-}MCC}, so hallucinated predictions on negative queries are penalized. We average each metric over the seven subsets, so mean cgF1 need not equal mean pmF1 times mean IL-MCC.

Geometry.

Table 22 lists the final evaluation splits. Unless a caption specifies a smaller set, depth ablations use all five depth benchmarks and normal ablations all normal benchmarks except Sintel. Depth benchmarks use the image lists and reference depths distributed with Marigold [38].

Crops and valid-pixel masks.

For both inverse-gray and metric-RGB predictions, depth evaluation retains valid ground-truth pixels within the dataset-specific ranges in Table 22. NYUv2 uses the standard crop, rows 45–470 and columns 41–600. KITTI applies a bottom-centered ×3521216\!\times\!352 crop to the input and ground-truth depth, then scores rows 117–320 and columns 43–1171 within that cropped grid. All row and column ranges are zero-indexed and inclusive. ETH3D is scored at ×13602048\!\times\!1360, with nearest-neighbor resizing of depth, masks and predictions. DIODE combines its official mask with an edge filter: the summed absolute horizontal and vertical Sobel responses on metric depth must be at most 0.30.3. The same mask is used for alignment and scoring. After disparity-affine alignment, inverse-gray predictions are clipped to the dataset depth bounds; ETH3D uses the largest valid ground-truth depth in each image as its upper bound.

Normal evaluation uses the benchmark targets and masks. ScanNet and iBims-1 use float normal maps distributed with Marigold; the iBims-1 maps are DSINE plane fits to laser-scanner depth [2]. Target vectors must be finite and nonzero. The axis convention is fixed before evaluation and never fitted on test images.

Depth metrics and alignment.

For ground-truth camera-zz depth ziz_{i} and predicted depth z^i\hat{z}_{i} on the valid set Ω\Omega, with N=|Ω|N=|\Omega|, we report

AbsRel\displaystyle\mathrm{AbsRel} =1N​∑i∈Ω|z^i−zi|zi,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in\Omega}\frac{|\hat{z}_{i}-z_{i}|}{z_{i}}, (5)
δ1\displaystyle\delta_{1} =1N∑i∈Ω[max(z^izi,ziz^i)<1.25].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in\Omega}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\max\!\left(\frac{\hat{z}_{i}}{z_{i}},\frac{z_{i}}{\hat{z}_{i}}\right)<1.25\right]. (6)

Tables report δ1\delta_{1} in percent. AbsRel is a fraction in the ablations and a percentage in Table 24. We obtain inverse-gray predictions pip_{i} by converting generated RGB to 8-bit grayscale (Pillow mode L) and dividing by 255. We fit a scale and shift by least squares, a​pi+b≈1/ziap_{i}+b\approx 1/z_{i}, on each image’s valid pixels. We clamp the fitted disparity below at 10−610^{-6}, invert it and clip the resulting depth before scoring on the same pixels. The metric-RGB ablation instead decodes RGB to depth and fits scale and shift in log-depth with RANSAC, following Marigold V2 [70]. It clips aligned depth to [10−3,maxi∈Ω⁡zi][10^{-3},\max_{i\in\Omega}z_{i}] m. Both protocols measure relative depth after ground-truth-assisted alignment, not recovery of absolute distance.

Surface normals.

We bilinearly resize generated RGB to the ground-truth grid, decode it using Eq. 2, and normalize prediction and target vectors. For each valid pixel, the angular error in degrees is

ei=180π​arccos⁡(clip⁡(𝐧^i⊤​𝐧i,−1,1)).e_{i}=\frac{180}{\pi}\arccos\!\left(\operatorname{clip}(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{n}_{i},-1,1)\right). (7)

Final-model tables report mean angular error and the percentage below 11.25∘11.25^{\circ}. Ablation tables report mean and median error. Predictions with a non-finite decoded norm or a norm below 0.010.01 receive a 90∘90^{\circ} error and remain included in all reported metrics.

Aggregation and ranking.

We average per-image metrics within each dataset. Thus, the reported normal median is the mean of the per-image medians, not a median over pooled pixels. Geometry averages weight datasets equally and use the same dataset intersection for all variants in a comparison. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best values, ranked before rounding unless a caption specifies otherwise.

C.4 Evaluation sets

Final models are evaluated on the complete evaluation sets listed in Table 21. Because the design-choice analyses only compare variants with each other, they use cheaper subsets of COCO-Stuff, COCO-Things and SA-Co/Gold. COCO-Stuff and COCO-Things use the first 500 validation images in order of image ID, scored on their 15 and 12 super-categories. For SA-Co/Gold, we sample 2,000 instance-exhaustive queries from each of its seven subsets (seed 0), giving 14K queries, and reuse the same presence-gate decisions in all comparisons. Geometry studies use the splits of Appendix E.2. Studies that deviate from these defaults state their evaluation sets in their setup or caption.

Development examples.

The validity-mask examples in Figure 13 come from an earlier development suite with different depth bounds and splits. That suite used ETH3D two-view training scenes, already-cropped KITTI depth-selection frames, nuScenes CAM_FRONT validation images with projected-LiDAR validity, and Virtual KITTI 2 clone views from camera 0. Its settings do not apply to the final evaluations in Table 22. Figure 22 instead uses the final zero-shot 9B model and benchmark targets.

Appendix D Additional Results

This section shows extended evaluations with the final OVB models.

D.1 Legend pruning on COCO-Object

Because accuracy drops as more classes are requested (Sec. E.1.1), legend pruning first asks an MLLM which of the 80 categories appear in the image and prompts OVB only with those. Pruning raises the mean single-pass mIoU of the zero-shot 9B model from 38.7 to 62.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and to 63.5 with Gemma4 31B, and that of the non-zero-shot model from 45.0 to 65.2 and 66.1 (Tabs. 2 and 23). Both zero-shot and non-zero-shot OVB 9B models score above the listed specialists.

D.2 Confidence estimates from vote agreement

We define the vote agreement of a pixel as the fraction of passes that vote for the majority class, counted over the passes that assign the pixel a class. It requires no additional computation and serves as a per-pixel confidence estimate. We evaluate it for the zero-shot OVB 9B on the Cityscapes validation set with R=30R{=}30, counting unassigned pixels as errors. Pixels with agreement ≥0.9\geq 0.9 cover 93.7% of the labeled pixels, and 97.8% of them are classified correctly. The remaining 6.3% of pixels have agreement below 0.9; 44.9% of them are misclassified, and they hold 57.6% of all errors in the validation set. These low-agreement pixels concentrate at class boundaries: 37.8% of them lie within 2 pixels of a ground-truth class boundary, whereas only 7.2% of all labeled pixels do. Agreement measures the consistency of the passes: it ranks pixels by reliability and should not be read as a calibrated probability of being correct. Figure 10 shows agreement maps for the two images of Fig. 7.

D.3 Full final-model geometry results

Tables 24 and 25 extend Tab. 8 with more benchmarks and published specialists. We evaluate the same four merged models as in Tab. 1 (Sec. C.1).

We evaluate geometry with the training prompts (pixel-explicit inverse depth and concise normals; Sec. F.2) and generation seed 0. Depth generation uses the preprocessed input dimensions instead of the 512-pixel training buckets: ×6721008\!\times\!672 for ETH3D and the input crop size for KITTI. Normal predictions are resized to the reference grid before decoding. Masks, alignment and scoring follow Sec. C.3.

Paired geometry examples.

Figure 11 compares the selected 9B models using the same prompts and inference settings as above. The NYUv2 depth and ScanNet normal examples were selected by visual inspection; the latter includes an artifact case. The KITTI depth and NYUv2 normal examples have the median zero-shot error within fixed sets of 20 candidate images, not within the full benchmarks.

Appendix E Extended Analysis of Design Choices

This appendix extends the design-choice analysis in Sec. 4. Its studies use ablation checkpoints rather than the selected models of Appendix D, so scores are compared only within each study.

E.1 Segmentation

These studies examine how the requested categories and instance-color conventions affect segmentation.

E.1.1 Number of requested classes

RQ-S3. How does accuracy change with the number of requested foreground classes?

For each requested class count KK, we evaluate the Top-64 palette model of Sec. 4.1 (Tab. 13) and request min⁡(K,pi)\min(K,p_{i}) classes per image, drawn uniformly at random from the pip_{i} foreground classes present in image ii. The class draw is seeded per image, so the legends are fixed for a given KK. The generation seed is fixed as well.

Unlike the set evaluation protocol, which requests random strict-subset, large KK can request all present classes. As in the protocol, only pixels of requested classes are scored, so predictions in unrequested regions are not penalized. Cityscapes uses 500 images, COCO-Stuff and COCO-Things use 493 and 496 after excluding images with no foreground classes. The largest present foreground class counts are 16, 9 and 6, respectively. Larger requests repeat the full-set condition (requesting all classes present in each image), so the curves plateau beyond these counts. Fig. 12 plots mIoU against KK for the three benchmarks.

Cityscapes falls from 82.9 mIoU at K=1K{=}1 to 71.0 at K=16K{=}16. Both COCO datasets also score lower at their largest requests than at K=1K{=}1. Requesting fewer classes therefore helps, which motivates the legend pruning of Sec. D.1.

E.1.2 Instance colors and prompts

RQ-S4. How should instance colors, ordering and prompts be chosen?

All variants use the same 32 separated named colors and matched training and evaluation conventions. We vary fixed versus random assignments, spatial ordering, and whether the prompt lists assignments, states only an ordering rule, or leaves both unstated.

As can be seen in Tab. 27, with stated top-to-bottom assignments, fixed colors beat random ones by 1.61 cgF1 (32.43 vs. 30.82), while random, unordered, unstated assignments reach 33.94. Changing the fixed scan to left-to-right raises cgF1 from 32.43 to 34.32. Fixed top-to-bottom assignments with only the ordering rule stated score highest, 34.72. MCC stays between 0.80 and 0.82. We nevertheless adopt fixed left-to-right assignments, stated in full, as the default: the gap to the implicit variant is 0.40 cgF1, that variant also changes the scan direction, and a stated legend fixes the instance-to-color mapping explicitly rather than relying on the model to apply the rule. Scan direction and prompt wording thus matter at least as much as color randomization.

E.2 Geometry

These studies use the reduced geometry training setup of Sec. 4. Evaluation follows Sec. C.3. Other-task scores measure retention in the same checkpoints.

E.2.1 Prompt and representation

RQ-S5. How do prompts and output representations affect geometry accuracy?

For each task, we train a separate 37.5K-step model for each prompt: concise, pixel-explicit and scene-preserving. Each run assigns the full 30% geometry share to that task. All three depth prompts use inverse-gray targets; a fourth depth run pairs the scene-preserving prompt with metric-RGB targets. All normal runs use canonical RGB targets. Each checkpoint is evaluated with its training prompt. Exact instructions appear in Sec. F.2.

Pixel-explicit wording gives the lowest depth AbsRel and normal errors, although normal means differ by less than 0.4∘0.4^{\circ}. Pixel-explicit and scene-preserving depth δ1\delta_{1} both round to 96.4%. Metric RGB improves neither depth metric under its corresponding alignment. The full-scale models use the concise normal prompt selected in an earlier 20K-step study; its mean error here is 0.3∘0.3^{\circ} higher than pixel-explicit.

E.2.2 Supervision and task mixture

Table 29(a) varies one training choice at a time from a 37.5K-step reference run with validity masks. Training masks follow Sec. 2.4; evaluation masks remain fixed. Erosion removes valid pixels within eight pixels of an invalid region before projection to the latent grid.

Validity masking improves both geometry tasks; eight-pixel erosion gives no additional gain at this budget.

Source-removal runs redistribute the omitted source’s probability equally among the remaining sources within each geometry task, keeping total geometry sampling probability at 30%. Source removal often trades depth against normal accuracy; no exclusion improves both depth metrics and normal mean error.

The allocation study changes only the division of the 30% geometry budget. The 10/20 depth/normal allocation improves normals relative to 20/10 but worsens depth and several retention scores. Full-scale training uses 10/20 (Table 20), fixed before this reduced-budget comparison favored 20/10. These results do not establish the best allocation at full scale.

E.2.3 Training duration

RQ-T1. How does performance change with training duration?

We compare 10K, 37.5K and 50K checkpoints under the same data, prompts, masks and optimization settings (Table 29(b)). Depth improves through 50K, whereas normal error is lowest at 37.5K. The 50K checkpoint leads all retention metrics except instance segmentation, which favors 37.5K.

E.2.4 Combined choices and seed variation

Table 29(c) starts from a separately trained 50K-step reference using the duration-study recipe: 20/10 allocation, all five sources, uneroded validity masks, pixel-explicit depth and concise normals. We add the listed changes cumulatively. Neither switching to 10/20 nor then adding erosion improves geometry. The full combination also removes Replica depth and Synscapes normals; all three seeds lower normal error but raise depth error. Only this combination was repeated, so the normal gain cannot be separated from variation between reference runs.

E.2.5 Replay and perception-data diversity

RQ-D2. How much replay and perception-data diversity are required?

Table 31 compares two 37.5K-step studies. The first varies the replay fraction from a 40% reference, keeping generation, editing and identity at a 3:3:2 ratio and allocating the remaining probability to perception tasks. The second varies the perception pool size through deterministic nested subsets at fixed task probabilities. Lower replay improves depth relative to 40%, but editing declines at 1% and the preferred fraction varies by metric. The full perception pool gives the lowest depth AbsRel and normal mean error, while some retention metrics favor smaller pools.

E.3 Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

Full fine-tuning of the 4B model needs 16 GH200 GPUs for about three days (Sec. 2.4). To test whether the recipe transfers to a parameter-efficient setting, we train LoRA adapters [34] on F2K4B Base with the zero-shot mixture and evaluate them with the protocol of Sec. C.3.

Setup.

All adapters are trained on the full zero-shot pool (Tab. 21). Each run attaches a LoRA adapter to every linear layer of the transformer, with scale α/r=1\alpha/r=1. The base weights stay frozen in bf16 and the adapters are trained in fp32. Optimizer, schedule, resolution buckets and the 1M-sample epochs follow Tab. 17, with 500 warm-up steps. Because the base weights are frozen, we use plain data parallelism instead of FSDP, with 4 samples per GPU on 16 GPUs (global batch 64) and a peak memory of 66 GiB per GPU. A 37.5K-step run takes about 9 h on 16 GH200 GPUs, and the same recipe should also fit, more slowly, on a single 4-GPU node with 4-step gradient accumulation. Each result is a single evaluation run with the fixed seeds of the evaluation protocol. A rank-256 learning-rate sweep found 33–×10−55\!\times\!10^{-5} usable; 10−410^{-4} and above degrade or diverge, while 10−510^{-5} learns too slowly. All runs below use ×10−55\!\times\!10^{-5}.

Rank and training length.

Table 32 compares ranks 64 to 1024 at 37.5K steps and continues ranks 64, 128 and 256 to 100K. At 37.5K, ranks 64 and 128 are the best adapters on all tasks except Cityscapes, and ranks 512 and 1024 are worse on nearly every task. With 102M–203M trainable parameters, ranks 64 and 128 match or exceed full fine-tuning at the same step count on image editing, depth and surface normals, trail it by 2–7 points on referring, reasoning and instance segmentation, and trail most on semantic segmentation. Longer training improves semantic segmentation for ranks 64 and 128, and beyond 50K it hurts rank 256 on most tasks. Because full fine-tuning uses a three times larger batch, we also compare the 100K-step adapters with the 37.5K-step full fine-tuning checkpoint, which has seen a similar number of samples. The best adapter still trails it by 5 mIoU on Cityscapes and 4 on COCO-Object, but is close on image editing and better on depth and normals. Overall, LoRA recovers most of the editing and geometry ability of OVB with a fraction of the trainable parameters, while dense semantic segmentation benefits most from updating all weights.

Appendix F Prompt Definitions

This section records the model-facing prompt families used across tasks.

F.1 Prompts for 2D tasks

Semantic segmentation.

Each prompt begins with [TASK: SEMANTIC_SEGMENTATION], followed by one of ten templates sampled with equal probability. The complete prompt therefore reads

Six dictionary-style templates embed the class–color mapping as a legend {legend} of the form {"road": "sky blue", "car": "red", ...}:

Four sentence-style templates consist of a lead-in followed by one clause per requested class:

Each prompt writes all of its colors in one notation: an everyday color name (e.g., sky blue), an RGB list (e.g., [220,30,30]), or a hexadecimal code (e.g., #DC1E1E). In dictionary legends, names are quoted, whereas RGB and hexadecimal values are not. The notation is sampled uniformly per prompt; names are unavailable when the legend exceeds the 37-color named palette. Only the first four dictionary templates state that unlisted pixels are black, but the target renders them black for every template. The released per-example manifest stores the fully rendered prompt.

Referring segmentation.

Each prompt begins with [TASK: REFERRING_SEGMENTATION], followed by one of three templates sampled uniformly. So, the complete prompt structure is

Here, {expression} is the referring expression, {color} a color name sampled from the 37-color named palette, and {rgb} its RGB value (e.g., [220,30,30]):

All three templates specify a black background; the third names the foreground color without its RGB value.

Instance segmentation.

Each prompt begins with [TASK: INSTANCE_SEGMENTATION], followed by one of four base templates (sampled uniformly) and the instance mapping ⟨\langleinstance mapping⟩\rangle. The complete prompt is

. The base templates are:

⟨\langleinstance mapping⟩\rangle:

The order of the 32 colors is the same for every training example and single-pass evaluation, and legend ensembling permutes it across passes.

Image editing, text-to-image generation, and identity.

Image-editing prompts preserve each Pico-Banana instruction and prepend the task tag when it is absent:

Text-to-image examples use the normalized PD12M caption without a task tag or fixed wrapper. Identity reconstruction uses a fixed instruction:

Evaluation prompts.

COCO-Object evaluation samples the semantic-segmentation templates above in RGB notation, SA-Co/Gold evaluation uses the instance-segmentation templates above, and depth and normal evaluation use the training prompts of Sec. F.2. Cityscapes and the two referring benchmarks use dedicated prompts. Cityscapes lists all 19 classes in a fixed order, with a new random color draw ({rgb}, e.g., [220,30,30]) per image:

RefCOCOg and ReasonSeg use the following prompt, where {color} is a sampled color name followed by its RGB value (e.g., red [220, 30, 30]) and, for ReasonSeg, {expression} is the original or rewritten query:

F.2 Exact geometry prompts

Full-scale models use pixel-explicit inverse depth and concise normals for both training and evaluation.

Depth: concise inverse.
Depth: pixel-explicit inverse.
